passages.t: Waters from the north over the Philistines
passages.happening:
This is the word of the LORD to Jeremiah about the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck Gaza (verse 1). Waters are rising from the north, an overflowing torrent that will flood the land, its towns and all who live there, and people will cry out (verse 2). At the sound of galloping stallions and rumbling chariots, ‘The fathers will not turn back for their sons; their hands will hang limp’ (verse 3).

The day has come to destroy the Philistines and to cut off every ally left to Tyre and Sidon (verse 4). Gaza will shave its head in mourning, and Ashkelon will be silenced; how long will the survivors of the valley cut themselves in grief (verse 5)?

Then a cry to the sword itself. ‘Alas, O sword of the LORD, how long until you rest? Return to your sheath; cease and be still’ (verse 6). But how can it rest when the LORD has given it orders against Ashkelon and the coast (verse 7)?
passages.hearers:
The Philistines lived in the cities of the coastal plain west of Judah, among them Gaza and Ashkelon. They were Israel's old neighbors and enemies from the days of Samson, Saul and David.

The heading dates the oracle before Pharaoh struck Gaza, without saying which pharaoh or when. Neco II campaigned along the coast around 609 BC, and may have attacked Gaza again around 601 BC; others suggest a later pharaoh. The poem itself speaks of an enemy from the north, usually taken as Babylon. The Babylonian Chronicle records that in the winter of 604 BC Nebuchadnezzar marched to Ashkelon, captured it, took its king prisoner and destroyed the city. Excavations at Ashkelon led by Lawrence Stager uncovered a thick destruction layer from that time.

Fathers too terrified to turn back for their children is the poem's picture of total panic. The cry to the sword to rest is almost a cry of pity.
passages.later: Amos had pronounced judgment on Gaza a century before (Amos 1:6-7), and Zephaniah said, ‘Gaza will be abandoned, and Ashkelon left in ruins’ (Zephaniah 2:4). Zechariah foresaw a remnant of them becoming ‘like a clan in Judah’ (Zechariah 9:7).
passages.hard:
The heading mentions Pharaoh striking Gaza, but the poem speaks of an enemy from the north. Do the two fit together?

Interpreters answer in different ways. One view is that the heading only dates the oracle, saying when Jeremiah spoke it, before an Egyptian attack on Gaza, while the poem foretells a different disaster from the north, Babylon; on this view the destruction of Ashkelon in 604 BC is a likely fulfillment. Another view is that the northern enemy could describe an army coming down the coast from Syria, as Egypt's army also did when returning from the north. Some scholars suggest the heading was added later. The text does not settle it.

The Philistines and their cities here are ancient peoples and places of the sixth century BC. These notes draw no line from this chapter to any people, place or conflict of the present day.
passages.asks: Even the prophet cries to the sword to rest. Ask whether you can grieve for a people who were long your enemies. And ask what it means that God's judgment on others is not a cause for celebration.
